title: Centripetal force
examples: What is the difference between centripetal force and centrifugal force?
How does the speed affect the required centripetal force in a loop-the-loop ride?
Can you give an example of centripetal force in everyday life?

explain.say: Today we look at the force keeping things in a circle. This force is called centripetal force.
The formula for this force uses the square of the speed. This is written as v squared divided by r.
Sometimes we use angular speed instead of linear speed. This is represented by the Greek letter omega, or omega.

items: Meaning | m times omega squared times r

explain.say: The force providing this must always point towards the center. Gravity or tension often provide this force.
Consider a ball swung on a string around your head. The tension in the string provides the centripetal force.
When you go down a roller coaster loop, gravity provides the necessary centripetal force. This is a real-life example.

faq.q: Does the mass of the object matter for the force?
faq.a: Yes, the mass of the object is directly proportional to the required centripetal force. If you double the mass, you double the force.
asks: Does heavier objects need more force?

faq.q: If I increase my speed, what happens to the force?
faq.a: Since the speed is squared in the formula, increasing the speed significantly increases the required centripetal force. This means you need much more force.
asks: If I go faster, is the force bigger?

faq.q: Is centrifugal force a real force?
faq.a: No, centrifugal force is not a real force. It is an apparent outward force that we feel when moving in a circle. The real force is always inward.
asks: What is the difference between centripetal and centrifugal?

faq.q: What is the relationship between linear and angular speed?
faq.a: They are related by the radius of the circular path. The linear speed is the radius times the angular speed. Think of it as a conversion factor.
asks: How do I use omega and v together?
What is the link between the two speeds?

faq.q: Does the radius affect the force?
faq.a: Yes, the force is inversely proportional to the radius. If you double the radius while keeping speed constant, you only need half the force.
asks: What if the circle gets bigger?
Does a larger radius mean less force?

facts: Centripetal force always directs the object toward the center of the circular path.
The required force is proportional to the square of the speed, written as v squared.
The formula using angular speed is Fc = m times omega squared times r.
Tension in a string can provide the necessary centripetal force.

quiz.say: A satellite orbits Earth at a constant speed. What provides the centripetal force?
quiz.why: Gravity between the two masses constantly pulls the satellite toward the center of the Earth.

wrong.0: Tension is only relevant if the satellite were attached to a string.
wrong.1: Inertia is a property of mass, not a physical force.
wrong.2: Centrifugal force is an apparent force, not the actual force acting on the satellite.

quiz.say: If you double the speed of a rotating object while keeping the radius the same, how does the required force change?
quiz.why: Because the speed is squared in the formula, doubling the speed results in a factor of two squared, which is four.

wrong.1: This mistake ignores the squared relationship in the formula.
wrong.2: This suggests an inverse relationship with speed.
wrong.3: This incorrectly applies the squaring to the wrong variable.

quiz.say: A car rounds a corner on a flat road. Which force provides the centripetal force?
quiz.why: The static friction between the tires and the road surface pushes the car toward the center of the curve.

wrong.1: The normal force acts perpendicular to the road surface, not horizontally into the curve.
wrong.2: The engine force propels the car forward, not sideways into the curve.
wrong.3: Gravity pulls the car straight down toward the Earth.
